keywords: Corn / maize maizium, maiziī n. Neo-Latin Stem quantity uncertain maizium, maiziī n. — maize; recorded in Morgan–Owens. This is an early modern Latin borrowing, not Classical vocabulary. maiza, maizae f. — another recorded modern form; frūmentum Indicum — an attested descriptive alternative. spīca, spīcae f. — ear of grain; extended to maize; grānum, grānī n. — grain or kernel; frūmentum, frūmentī n. — cereal grain collectively. The source establishes the word, not all its stem vowel lengths. Only the certain Latin inflectional quantity is marked in maiziī .

keywords: Vitamin vītamīnum, vītamīnī n. Neo-Latin Reading convention vītamīnum, vītamīnī n. — vitamin; a modern lexical form. The feminine variant vitamina, vitaminae f. is also recorded by Morgan–Owens, without documented stem quantities. vītamīna, vītamīnōrum n. pl. — vitamins, using the neuter form. vītamīnicus, vītamīnica, vītamīnicum — pertaining to vitamins; a transparent derivative, not claimed here to be corpus-verified. For a multivitamin preparation, praeparātum plūra vītamīna continēns is an explicit description; the previous unsupported claim for multivītamīnum has been withdrawn. Hic cibus multa vītamīna continet. — This food contains many vitamins. The international term was coined from “vita” and “amine”; it does not imply that all vitamins are amines. The ī in vīta and the adopted international -amīn- reading give our convention vītamīnum ; these are reconstructed Neo-Latin reading quantities, not attested Classical measurements.

Ancient dictionaries also record other forms. sūcus citreī — lemon juice. Paulum cinnamōmī adde. — Add a little cinnamon. Traupman records citreum for lemon. Morgan–Owens distinguishes its ancient citron reference from the later lemon use. The herbs and spices have ancient lexical names, without requiring every ancient species identification to equal a modern supermarket label.
